title: Characterizing Quantum Advantage for Generalizations of the Boolean Hidden Matching Problem
authors: Mark Bun, Joao F. Doriguello, John Kallaugher, Nadezhda Voronova
abstract: We study the one-way communication complexity of the $f$-Boolean Hidden Partition problem. Here, Alice is given an $n$-bit string and Bob is given $Ω(n)$ disjoint blocks of its indices together with a string of labels. Under the promise that the evaluations of $f$ on these blocks either agree with all of the labels or disagree with all of them, Bob must determine which is the case using a single message from Alice. This problem generalizes the Boolean Hidden Matching and Hidden Hypermatching problems, which capture the special case where $f$ is the parity function.   We establish classical and quantum communication bounds for $f$-Boolean Hidden Partition in terms of the sign degree $d$ of $f$, proving a conjecture of Doriguello and Montanaro (TQC 2020). Their prior work gave logarithmic communication upper bounds for classical protocols when $d \le 1$ and quantum protocols when $d \le 2$, as well as polynomial lower bounds for certain structured functions with larger sign degree. We show that for every $f$ of sign degree $d \ge 2$, the randomized classical communication complexity of this problem is $Θ(n^{1-1/d})$ while its quantum communication complexity lies between $Ω(n^{1-2/d})$ and $\bO{n^{1-1/\lceil d/2 \rceil} \log n}$. This completely characterizes the functions $f$ admitting polynomial quantum advantage as those for which $d \ge 2$, with a new infinite family of exponential separations given by the case $d = 2$.
summary: This work analyzes the communication complexity of a generalized hidden matching problem, linking the computational difficulty directly to the sign degree of the underlying Boolean function $f$. It establishes precise classical and quantum communication bounds, proving that a polynomial quantum advantage exists if and only if the sign degree $d$ is two or greater. This provides a deep theoretical understanding of quantum computational separation in communication tasks.
main_problem: The paper characterizes the quantum advantage for solving generalizations of the Boolean Hidden Matching Problem, specifically the $f$-Boolean Hidden Partition problem.
main_result: The sign degree $d$ of the function $f$ completely characterizes the communication complexity, showing that quantum advantage exists if and only if $d \ge 2$.
method: The authors use Boolean Fourier analysis and hypercontractivity to establish rigorous classical and quantum communication lower bounds based on the sign degree $d$.
model_or_system: The model is the one-way communication complexity setting where Alice holds an $n$-bit string and Bob holds disjoint blocks of indices, requiring Bob to determine if function evaluations agree or disagree with given labels.
key_observables: Classical and quantum one-way communication complexity (in bits/qubits), and the sign degree $d$ of the function $f$.
important_parameters: The sign degree $d = 	ext{deg}_{\pm}(f)$, and the input size $n$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the promise that the function evaluations either all agree or all disagree with the labels, and it addresses scenarios where the independence assumption breaks down.
paper_structure: The paper establishes bounds by first analyzing the problem structure, then developing new tools using Fourier analysis to prove lower bounds dependent on $d$, and finally deriving upper bounds that match these lower bounds to achieve characterization.
why_interesting: The rigorous characterization of quantum advantage based on a purely algebraic property (sign degree) of a Boolean function is highly relevant for understanding the limits of quantum communication protocols.
